title: Cheap Prizes: We Didn’t Get into This for Those
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a conversation with a first-year teacher who gave everything to the job yet felt thankless, Stuart argues that praise, awards, favorite-teacher status and even public esteem for the profession are cheap prizes. Teachers did not enter the work for them, and they are as fickle as shifting sand dunes. What is really at stake each day is the chance to shift a life trajectory, to model excellence and kindness, and to be some small part of why students flourish. Stuart admits he fights the same hunger for affirmation himself. His move is to prescribe a hard internal interrogation (did you really get into teaching for that?) as part of the inner work of teaching, which keeps teachers sane and on the road to the teachers they hoped to be.
points: Awards, praise and favorite-teacher comments are reframed as cheap prizes that fickle opinion can give or withdraw.
The real stakes are life-trajectory lessons, a living model of how to be in the world, and a small share in students' long-term flourishing.
Stuart models honesty by admitting he shares the drive for external affirmation.
Challenging one's own motives is named as the inner work of teaching and a guard against resentment.
quotes: The awards, praises, and “favorite teacher” comments are cheap prizes. We did not get into teaching for these things.
That drive to prove himself, to receive external affirmation for what he's doing in the classroom, to be seen as remarkably good at this work: those demons are regulars around here.
And part of that is because public opinion and this year's eval rubric are fickle, here today and changed tomorrow. Like shifting sand dunes, they have impermanence woven into them.
Over a school year, who knows that we could be 1% of the reasons why our students go on to lead flourishing lives?

These don't get tied to merit pay, and they probably won't show up on the end of year test. But they're why we got in; we have to hold to them, even as we pursue the student achievement results our stakeholders desire.

It's these conversations with ourselves, these moments of hard internal interrogation, that keep us on the road to becoming the teachers we always hoped we'd be and staying sane in the process. This is part of the inner work of teaching.
